vignette: Mara, a 63-year-old Oceania woman and project manager, has struggled with the aftermath of her life-threatening illness. Her experiences during that time have left deep scars that affect nearly every aspect of her daily life. The traumatic event was a harrowing experience, one that involved prolonged hospitalization where she endured multiple medical procedures and treatments. During those days, she felt overwhelmed by the sight of needles and other medical equipment, the constant touch from healthcare providers, and the conversations about her condition that seemed to strip away any sense of control or normalcy. Mara's triggers are now a significant part of her daily life. Certain conversation topics related to her illness can quickly escalate her irritability. When she hears others discuss similar experiences, it feels like an insurmountable weight pressing down on her. Her body reacts almost instantly; she becomes agitated and angry outbursts are not uncommon. This irritability is heightened when she encounters medical equipment or undergoes examinations. The sight of needles or the sound of medical machinery in a clinic can send her into a state of alarm, making it difficult to concentrate on anything else. One day at work, while discussing project timelines with a colleague, Mara was reminded of the time she had been rushed into surgery without much notice. Her body tensed up, and she felt her heart pounding. She reacted sharply, unable to articulate why her irritation was so intense in that moment. The memory came back vividly-she could feel every sensation as if it were happening again, reliving the fear and helplessness of that time. The intensity of these memories is further exacerbated by Mara's belief that her life has been irrevocably altered. She feels ashamed about what happened to her body and cannot trust herself or her own physical experiences anymore. These negative appraisals have seeped into her daily functioning, making it nearly impossible for her to engage in activities she once enjoyed without being overwhelmed by the memories of her illness. When Mara tries to talk about what happened, she finds that she cannot put the experience into words. The memory is more of a sensory reliving-a vivid reenactment where her body feels as if it's back in those moments of fear and uncertainty. This inability to verbalize her experiences only reinforces her negative appraisals. She believes her life has been destroyed, and this belief makes it harder for her to cope with the triggers that constantly remind her of what happened. Her concentration suffers greatly because of these intense reactions. At work, she finds herself distracted by thoughts and memories that can make even simple tasks seem overwhelming. Her irritability often affects her relationships at home as well; her husband has noticed a change in how she interacts with him and others. The more Mara feels threatened, the stronger her memory becomes-a cycle that seems to tighten around her daily life. She is certain that her body will betray her again, leading to more frequent reliving of those terrifying moments. The memory triggers more negative appraisals, which then heighten her threat response even further. It was a particularly stressful day at work when Mara realized she needed help. Her irritability had become so intense that she snapped at a colleague over something trivial, and the guilt afterward pushed her to seek support. What frightens her most is losing control of herself and her life completely. She hopes for relief from these overwhelming memories and the ability to regain some semblance of normalcy in her daily experiences. Mara's current state is one of constant vigilance and heightened reactivity, but she is determined to find a way through it.
